blocks.text: Former Australia coach Darren Lehmann has again vehemently denied any knowledge of the sandpaper plot, despite detailed allegations from Cameron Bancroft.

In an ongoing row about the cheating scandal that took place in Australia's third Test against South Africa in 2018, Bancroft published a testimony running to more than 4,000 words in the West Australian newspaper on Wednesday.
At the same time, Lehmann was commentating on Australia's third one-day international against England, with Bancroft's account prompting him to leave the match early.
On Saturday, Lehmann returned to broadcast for the BBC and Australian network ABC on the first T20 international in Melbourne.
In an extended and emotional interview, addressing a range of Bancroft's claims, Lehmann said:
He "didn't know" sandpaper was used by his Australia team
No coaches encouraged players to tamper with the ball before or during Australia's tour of South Africa in 2018
He is "not sure" about a walkie-talkie conversation with 12th man Peter Handscomb, which Bancroft claimed was an instruction from Lehmann to remove the sandpaper from the field
He resigned as Australia coach before he was sacked and did not sign a non-disclosure agreement
The fallout from the sandpaper scandal took him to a "really dark place".

Lehmann's renewed denial came on the same day Cricket Australia confirmed its "unanimous support" for Pat Cummins as Australia captain.
Earlier, Cummins' fellow fast bowler Josh Hazlewood said he would consider his international future if the captain is forced to stand down.
The debate about the sandpaper plot of 2018 was reopened two weeks ago by allegations in the autobiography of Usman Khawaja, who was part of the Australia team in Cape Town eight years ago.
Khawaja's assertions the whole team knew and should have taken responsibility have been supported by David Warner, Chadd Sayers and Jon Holland, who were all on the tour.

Warner, former captain Steve Smith and Bancroft were the only players punished for the cheating plot. It was Bancroft's testimony that heaped pressure on Lehmann, Cummins and the other members of the Australia team who played at Newlands.
Cummins, Hazlewood and the rest of the Australia bowlers who played in Cape Town have always denied knowledge or involvement in the plan to use sandpaper on the ball.
Lehmann resigned as coach in the immediate aftermath of the South Africa tour, but the former Australia batter has always maintained his innocence.
"Sandpaper, I didn't know," he said on Saturday. "Obviously, it was used.
"The biggest thing with ball-tampering is it was just a bad time. Everyone, we all made mistakes.
"But you've just got to try and move on. I know it's hard for everyone. The game of cricket is bigger than any individual team. We're custodians of the baggy green and we got a few things wrong."
Bancroft was caught on camera during the third Test between Australia and South Africa, yet alleged the use of sandpaper had begun during the second Test.
In Cape Town, TV pictures showed Bancroft hiding the sandpaper in his trousers. In his account, Bancroft alleged Lehmann immediately told Handscomb to "get the sandpaper off Bangers now".
Responding to that allegation, Lehmann said: "I'm not sure. That was all after the fact. It was already played out on TV.
"That's Cameron's take on it. I'm not going to talk about him, but my view is different."

In his version, Khawaja asserted the players were encouraged before the South Africa series to get the ball swinging by any means necessary. Both Khawaja and Bancroft agreed players were further emboldened to cheat by coaches during the tour.
Bancroft elaborated further, saying the whole playing squad and coaches openly discussed and even celebrated the effect of using sandpaper during the second Test.
Lehmann said: "No, I don't understand that statement as such, because at the end of the day, I didn't get that statement. I didn't get that question posed to me.
"I can't comment for anyone else. Again, because I said before, I can only comment on what I know."
Bancroft also described the origin of the sandpaper idea, which he claimed was thought up by Warner at tea on the second day of the second Test.
Lehmann countered: "I can't remember that conversation. Again, eight and a half years ago. You'd have to ask those people.
"That's the issue. I have my version and that's where I stand."
Lehmann is currently head coach of Northamptonshire. In 2020, two years after the sandpaper saga, he had heart bypass surgery after falling ill on his 50th birthday.

'I went to a really dark place'
Lehmann was asked by ABC's Matt Clinch about the physical and mental toll of the sandpaper saga and the full answers are below:
I mean, I can tell you this. Eight and a half years ago, and I don't like talking about this sort of scenario, but I went to a really dark place. As dark a place as you can think about.
It took me, and this is just me, probably three or four years to actually get back to some sort of normality.
To the stage where we are now, I'm not going back to that. I'm trying to move forward. I'm not going back.
There's things I remember and don't remember. It's eight and a half years ago. It was a traumatic time, none more so for my family.
Without the support of family and friends back then, I don't know where I'd be.
And that's the same with the family and friends, and even Northamptonshire this year, who've been a second family over the last three or four years. They've been outstanding.
The support and messages I've got in the last few days have been something that's kept me reasonable.
I feel for everyone at the moment and their families. Social media has been so vitriolic. The hatred is there. It's just unbelievable.
I've never seen anything like it since 2018. And the trauma for everyone is there to see again.
For me, being one of them, you just try and contact as many people as you can, stay in touch with them and try and put one foot forward as best you can.
Eight and a half years ago it was terrible for a lot of people. So to revisit where we are now is not great for a lot of people. That's sad.
Clinch then asked: "I don't want to ask you any inappropriate questions, but was that dark place a feeling of guilt over what you could have done differently?"
Could have done a lot of things differently.
I can only speak for me. I wish we did things differently and we didn't push the boundaries too far. We didn't get to the stage where we got to.
I've just got to take responsibility for that. That's where I'm at.
We're talking about people's livelihoods and how they can move forward mentally, physically, be happy again.
I want to see people be happy again. That doesn't look like we're there at the moment, does it?
Some of the things that are being said are just outright hurtful to a lot of people.
That's what I care about. I care about everyone. There's a lot of people being hurt at the moment and I think people have forgotten about that aspect.
Yes, there were mistakes. You apologise as best you can, you try and move on. That's sort of where I'm at, mate.
Again, I'm not going back to that place. I don't want to.
It feels like everyone's pushing you on to these bad places.
Some of my colleagues with ABC and some other friendly journalists have checked in, which I really appreciate.
But then you have people who haven't checked in who you thought would have. And then people making comments on you when they don't even know you for a start.
It hurts your families more. The families are the bigger picture in all this.
It's a big game and they do as many jobs as they can [unclear].
I think the way the team's evolved, and I think they've been to these press conferences and evolved, they're happy where they are and they've worked hard on everything to be the best they can be.
And that goes for a lot of people. That goes for me eight and a half years ago, that person I don't want to go back to, to this person now.
I hope people respect that as best they can, really, mate. I hope you respect that.
I hope people can respect that everyone's going through a tough time and we just let the players play the game of cricket.
Because it's a wonderful game being played and I love seeing, walking around the parks and seeing the boys and girls trying to represent the baggy green.
